lead: A marine radio is licensed twice: the set through the boat, the operator through a certificate. The rules that come with them are few and mostly common sense: identify yourself, put distress first, send nothing you need not send, and repeat nothing you overhear.

sections.title: One for the boat, one for you

qa.q: What is the difference between a ship station licence and an SRC?
qa.a: The **ship station licence** belongs to the boat and lists her call sign, MMSI and radio equipment; the Short Range Certificate (SRC) belongs to you, the operator, whatever boat you sail. Keep both aboard.

blocks.p: The **ship station licence** belongs to the boat. It names the vessel and lists her call sign, her MMSI and the radio equipment she is licensed to carry. The **operator's certificate** belongs to a person: for VHF with DSC it is the **Short Range Certificate (SRC)**, while the **Long Range Certificate (LRC)** adds MF/HF and satellite. It shows that you are qualified to use the radio, and it is yours whatever boat you sail. Sell your yacht and buy another, and the certificate stays with you. The rules are ITU's; your flag state issues the licence, call sign and MMSI, and may add its own requirements.

fig.title: Ship station licence

blocks.p: On a charter yacht the licence is in the charter firm's name and covers the set; your certificate covers you as the operator. Keep both documents aboard: a port official inspecting the yacht may ask for them.

sections.title: The skipper decides, the certificate holder supervises

qa.q: Can crew without a radio certificate use the VHF on my yacht?
qa.a: Only **under the supervision** of a certificate holder, and as the skipper decides; alone they may not make a routine call. In distress, anyone aboard may send the MAYDAY.

blocks.p: The ship's radio station is under the **authority of the skipper**. Whether the crew may use it to chat with friends on another yacht is the skipper's decision.

Someone without a certificate may operate the radio **under the supervision** of a certificate holder. Alone, she may not make a routine call. Distress is the exception: when lives are in danger, anyone aboard may send the MAYDAY.

qa.q: Can I use the yacht's handheld VHF ashore, say from a taverna?
qa.a: No: a marine VHF is licensed for the **maritime service**, meaning use afloat, and use from land generally needs special permission. Afloat abroad is fine: the ship station licence is valid internationally, alongside local regulations.

blocks.p: A ship station licence is valid internationally. Your own yacht, licensed in her home country, may use her VHF in Greek waters, where you also follow the local regulations.

A marine VHF is licensed for the **maritime service**, which means use afloat. Taking the yacht's handheld to a taverna to call the crew on board is not allowed: use from land generally needs special permission.

fig.note: A handheld ashore is outside the maritime service

qa.q: What am I not allowed to transmit on marine VHF?
qa.a: **Prohibited transmissions** include a false distress call, even as a test; any call that does not give your own boat's name; unnecessary signals, such as clicking the key to say hello; and obscene or abusive language.

blocks.rule: Before you press the key: is it needed, is it true, and does it say who you are?

sections.title: Keep it to yourself, write it down

qa.q: Can I tell anyone about a VHF conversation I overheard?
qa.a: No: **secrecy of correspondence** means you may not pass on what you overhear. Distress traffic is the exception: if the coast station seems not to have heard a MAYDAY you noted, pass its details to the coastguard.

blocks.p: VHF is an open line, and you will overhear calls not meant for you. **Secrecy of correspondence** means you may not pass on what you overhear: two yachts' family matters stay with them. Distress traffic is the exception. If you noted a MAYDAY that the coast station seems not to have heard, pass its details to the coastguard.
Note in the log the distress, urgency and safety traffic you send or hear, with the times: it may be needed later.

qa.q: Which goes first when several messages are waiting for the channel?
qa.a: They go in a fixed **order of priority**, whoever was ready first: distress (MAYDAY), urgency (PAN-PAN), safety (SÉCURITÉ), then routine calls.

blocks.p: When several messages wait for a quiet channel, they go in a fixed order, whoever was ready first.
